clinical_knowledge.topic: Herpes Zoster Ophthalmicus evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Herpes Zoster Ophthalmicus is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management follows an evidence-based diagnostic and therapeutic protocol for Herpes Zoster Ophthalmicus, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.

common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Herpes Zoster Ophthalmicus.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Herpes simplex virus infection without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Vesicles on the tip or side of the nose (Hutchinson's sign) — high risk of ocular involvement and permanent vision damage.
management_principles: Start systemic antiviral therapy promptly (for example, oral valacyclovir when appropriate) and arrange urgent ophthalmology assessment for ocular involvement
Refer to specialty team and provide comprehensive patient counseling
Assess clinical stability, monitor vital parameters, and perform targeted diagnostic investigations.
Implement targeted therapeutic interventions per evidence-based clinical practice guidelines.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with symptoms of Herpes Zoster Ophthalmicus: severe burning pain followed by grouped vesicles on red base across forehead and tip of nose (Hutchinson sign). 64M presenting with painful unilateral dermatomal vesicular eruption along ophthalmic branch of V1 trigeminal nerve with vesicles on nasal tip (Hutchinson sign) requiring urgent Valacyclovir and ophthalmology exam for anterior uveitis.
reference_soap.objective: Complete vital signs and focused physical examination required. Diagnostic workup tailored for Herpes Zoster Ophthalmicus.
reference_soap.assessment: Clinical presentation highly suggestive of Herpes Zoster Ophthalmicus.
reference_soap.plan: Start systemic antiviral therapy promptly (for example, oral valacyclovir when appropriate), ideally within 72 hours of rash onset but without delaying treatment for suspected ophthalmic involvement. Arrange same-day urgent ophthalmology assessment to evaluate for keratitis, uveitis, and elevated intraocular pressure. Provide analgesia and counsel on urgent review for visual change, eye pain, or photophobia.

teaching.one_liner: Reactivation of varicella-zoster virus in the ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve, causing painful vesicles across the forehead — vesicles on the tip of the nose (Hutchinson's sign) predict eye involvement and need urgent ophthalmology evaluation.
red_flags: Vesicles on the tip or side of the nose (Hutchinson's sign) — high risk of ocular involvement and permanent vision damage

must_ask.say: Did the burning pain start before the blisters appeared?
Is the rash confined to one side of your forehead, and does it involve the tip of your nose?
Any eye pain, redness, or vision changes?
How many days ago did the rash appear?
Do you have any condition that weakens your immune system?

history.answer: My left forehead has been burning terribly, and yesterday these blistery bumps broke out across my forehead and the tip of my nose.
The intense burning and tingling started three days ago on my left forehead, and then the reddish bumps and fluid-filled blisters popped up yesterday morning.
It is strictly on the left side of my face, covering my left forehead, scalp, upper eyelid, and right on the tip of my nose without crossing over to the right side.
They look like clusters of small, watery blisters sitting on very red, inflamed skin.
Two days before the blisters appeared, my skin started tingling and then turned into a sharp, severe burning pain, which hurts even when a breeze touches it.
No, they have not faded or moved at all; they erupted yesterday and have stayed in the exact same spots.
No, I had chickenpox as a young boy, but I have never had shingles or a painful rash like this before.
I felt slightly feverish and fatigued with a dull headache when the burning started, but no severe chills.
My left eye feels gritty and looks somewhat red, and it is slightly sensitive to bright light, but I have no ulcers inside my mouth or groin.
No, the skin has not peeled off in sheets, and there are no dark purple bruised spots.
No swelling of my lips or tongue, no throat tightness, no wheezing, and no shortness of breath.
I have not started any new prescription drugs, antibiotics, or pain relievers recently; I have been on the same blood pressure pill for years.
No, I have not changed my face wash, soap, or shampoo, nor have I worn new jewelry or handled unfamiliar plants.
No one in my house has a rash or blisters, and nobody around me is sick.
No, I have not been hiking in the woods, had any bug bites, or traveled anywhere outside the city recently.
I do not have eczema, asthma, or hay fever.
My joints feel fine, and my fingernails have not changed or pitted.
I put a cool compress on my forehead for temporary relief, but I have not put any steroid or antifungal creams on it.
I am in a long-term monogamous marriage, and I have never had any genital sores or ulcers.
I do not have HIV or cancer, and I do not take steroid pills or chemotherapy, though work has been unusually stressful lately.
I thought a venomous spider bit me while I was sleeping, or maybe I brushed against some harsh weed killer or chemical in the garage.
I'm terrified that this blister outbreak is spreading right into my eye and that I'm going to go blind.
I want someone to examine my eye right away to make sure it's safe, and give me strong pills to knock out the infection and stop this unbearable burning.
I have high blood pressure and mildly elevated cholesterol, both monitored by my doctor.
I had an appendectomy when I was in college, with no other surgeries or hospitalizations.
I take lisinopril 10 milligrams every morning for my blood pressure.
I have no known drug allergies.
I have never smoked cigarettes in my life.
I drink one glass of red wine with dinner on weekends, never heavily.
I work as an accountant, live at home with my wife, and stay physically active by walking regularly.
My father had high blood pressure, but there is no family history of skin conditions or autoimmune diseases.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 128/82 mmHg, pulse 74 bpm, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, body temperature 36.8°C, oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Alert, oriented middle-aged male in mild to moderate discomfort due to left-sided facial and forehead burning pain.

Grouped clear vesicles and erythematous papules on an erythematous base strictly confined to the left forehead, scalp, upper eyelid, and left nasal tip (positive Hutchinson sign), respecting the facial midline.
Left conjunctival injection with mild ciliary flush; left cornea shows faint epithelial haze; visual acuity 20/25 in the left eye and 20/20 in the right eye.
Mild injection of the left bulbar conjunctiva; right conjunctiva clear; sclerae non-icteric bilaterally.
Small vesicles and crusting on the left nasal tip; oral and pharyngeal mucosa are pink, moist, and free of ulcers or vesicles.
Palpable tender preauricular and anterior cervical lymphadenopathy on the left side; right neck nodes are non-palpable.
Hyperesthesia and marked allodynia along the distribution of the left ophthalmic division (V1) of the trigeminal nerve; extraocular movements intact.
